feedback: If the digits are right but the magnitude is wrong (e.g. 5,300 or 53,00 for 45,000 + 8,000), name it as a place-value slip: re-slide 45 + 8 = 53 up the chart saying the unit each step so '53' becomes '53 thousand'.
If the learner recomputes from scratch at each scale instead of reusing the known fact, pause and ask 'which small fact is hiding inside this one?' before continuing.
activities.intendedInsight: A 'big' calculation is often a small fact the learner already owns, with place value shifting the whole fact up predictably; the zeros are bookkeeping, not extra arithmetic.
learnerActions: State a known small fact first, e.g. 6 + 4 = 10, then scale it up a place-value row at a time: 60 + 40 = 100, 600 + 400 = 1,000, 6,000 + 4,000 = 10,000, saying aloud how many zeros the answer gains.
Repeat the scaling with a fact that bridges, e.g. 45 + 8 = 53, to reach 450 + 80 = 530 and 45,000 + 8,000 = 53,000; say the unit explicitly ('45 thousand plus 8 thousand is 53 thousand').

Check each scaled answer keeps '53' as its non-zero digits and changes only in magnitude, matching the size of the numbers being added (530 is 53 tens; 53,000 is 53 thousands); flag an answer that loses that digit pattern (e.g. 125,000) or that keeps the digits but lands at the wrong magnitude (e.g. 5,300 instead of 53,000) as a scaling slip, not a new sum.
activities.title: Scaling bench: a small fact with zeros bolted on

feedback: If the learner gives the landing point instead of the total of the jumps, remind them the answer is the sum of the hops (800 + 6,000 = 6,800), not 10,000.
If the learner describes 'borrowing' across the zeros and pauses or errs, model the gap on a number line instead: frame it as measuring the distance between the two numbers.
For 20,000 - 19,850, if the learner starts a full decomposition, prompt 'how far apart are these two numbers?' to surface the single small jump of 150.
activities.intendedInsight: Subtraction from a round number is a short journey measured by adding the jumps; counting up avoids the error-prone mental 'borrowing' across a string of zeros, and the size of the gap signals when it is the smart choice.
learnerActions: Subtract 3,200 from 10,000 by counting up on an empty number line: jump +800 from 3,200 to 4,000, then +6,000 from 4,000 to 10,000; the answer is the TOTAL of the jumps, 6,800 (not the point you land on).
Try 20,000 - 19,850 the same way: notice the numbers are close, count up +150 from 19,850 to 20,000, and decide this gap is tiny so counting up is clearly quicker than decomposing.
Say aloud whether counting up or taking away felt easier for each, and why the numbers made that choice sensible.
activities.title: Counting up from a round number

feedback: If the learner reaches a correct answer by one slow default method throughout, accept the answer but ask 'what did you notice about these two numbers?' to prompt near-doubles or counting up.
If the learner cannot name any strategy, work one example together and have them re-explain it in their own words before the next item.
activities.intendedInsight: Efficient mental calculation is about reading the numbers and picking a strategy that fits them, not applying one default method to everything.
learnerActions: Look at 2,500 + 2,600 and spot the near-double: double 2,500 = 5,000, then add 100 to get 5,100, rather than partitioning digit by digit.
Sort a mixed set of calculations into 'count up' versus 'partition' versus 'near-double/compensate', saying what feature of the numbers triggered each choice.
After solving each item, explain the method used; compare a partitioning route and a near-doubles/counting-up route side by side for the same item to see which was fewer steps.
activities.title: Choosing a strategy to fit the numbers
